kurz: The entry is based on a guess, whereas the loss limit is set in advance, and it determines the number of units, the expected value and how long the capital can withstand losing periods.

bloecke.md:
At entry, everything rests on a forecast. The price at which a thesis is considered to have failed, by contrast, is set in advance. Together with the number of units, it is the only variable over which the trader has complete control. The calculation therefore begins with the question of how much this one trade may cost. How much there is to earn comes only after that.

The amount a trade may cost is called R. One R is what a position costs in the planned loss scenario, and it is neither its nominal volume nor the capital employed. If results are recorded in R-multiples instead of euros from now on, trades of different sizes, at different prices and in different markets can be compared. A gain of 2R always corresponds to twice the planned loss, regardless of whether the position was €1,500 or €12,000 in size.

bloecke.formel: Units = (Capital × Risk per trade) / (Entry − Stop price)
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula starts from the risk set in advance and derives the position size from it. The usual approach is the reverse order, in which the chosen position size determines the risk.
variablen: portfolio value to which the risk percentage refers
share of the capital that is lost if the trade ends in a loss; 0.5% to 2% is usual
price at which the position is closed without further review
bloecke.beispiel: €20,000 capital, 1% risk, entry €50.00, stop €47.00: (20,000 × 0.01) / 3.00 = 66 units (rounded down). The nominal volume is €3,300, and €198 is at risk.

bloecke.md: Stop distance and number of units are thus determined in a single decision. A tight stop automatically results in more units, a wide stop in fewer. The euro risk stays the same, but the nominal volume does not. With it, the risk from price gaps and the cost burden also change.

bloecke.titel: Four positions with the same euro risk (entry €50.00, risk €200)

bloecke.md:
A triggered stop-loss order becomes a market sell order and is executed at the next tradable price. If the security opens with a [[price gap]] well below the stop after a news announcement, it is sold at this lower price. The loss is then 2R or 3R instead of 1R. A stop-limit order prevents a sale at such a poor price. In return, it may not be executed at all, and the position remains open while the price continues to fall.

The first row of the table above therefore describes the riskiest position, even though its tight stop looks the most cautious. With 50% of the portfolio in one security, a price gap of 6% costs €600 instead of €200. Tight stops are therefore only justifiable if an upper limit is also placed on the position size.

## Stop distance based on volatility

A stop 3% below the entry has completely different effects on two different securities. For a calm blue chip, it lies far outside the daily fluctuation. For a volatile small cap, it is triggered by normal, random price movements before the thesis could even be tested. The distance is therefore usually derived from the measured volatility of the security.

The [[average true range]] (ATR) is suitable for this. It measures the typical price range of a period, including price gaps, and says nothing about direction. It is therefore of no use as a buy signal, but it works well as a yardstick for stop distances and position sizes.

bloecke.formel:
TR = max(High − Low, |High − Previous close|, |Low − Previous close|)
ATR(14) = (Previous ATR × 13 + Current TR) / 14
Stop price = Entry − k × ATR(14)
bloecke.erklaerung: The true range takes the largest of three values and therefore also captures price gaps. In practice, the factor k is usually between 1.5 and 3. The smaller k is, the more often the position is stopped out by random price fluctuations.
variablen: true range, the actual range of a period
smoothed average of the true range over 14 periods according to Wilder
bloecke.beispiel: With an entry of €50.00, ATR(14) = €0.80 and k = 2, the stop is at €48.40. The distance is €1.60 per unit.

bloecke.md:
Capital €20,000, risk per trade 1%, so R = €200. Both securities are trading at €50.00, and the stop is at 2 ATR in each case.

- Security A with ATR(14) = €0.80 has its stop at 48.40 and a distance of €1.60. Units = 200 / 1.60 = 125 units, nominal volume €6,250.
- Security B with ATR(14) = €2.50 has its stop at 45.00 and a distance of €5.00. Units = 200 / 5.00 = 40 units, nominal volume €2,000.

With the same price, capital and risk, the capital employed for security A is more than three times as high as for security B. Without this normalisation, both positions would look the same size, but in the portfolio security B would be many times more dangerous than security A.

bloecke.titel: Nominal volume at a constant risk of €200
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for a price of €50.00 and a stop at 2 ATR, in which the euro risk is the same in all cases and the position becomes larger the calmer the security is.

bloecke.md:
## Win rate and reward-to-risk ratio

Trading systems are almost always advertised with their win rate. On its own, this figure is worthless, because it says nothing about how large gains and losses are. A conclusion is only possible together with the [[reward-to-risk ratio]] (RRR), the expected gain in R-multiples.

A strategy with an 80% win rate and an RRR of 0.2 loses money, because four gains of 0.2R each bring in less in total than one loss of 1R costs. A strategy with a 35% win rate and an RRR of 3, by contrast, makes substantial profits. Trend-following systems work according to the second pattern. With them, two out of three trades end in a loss, which is why they feel wrong to the people using them.

bloecke.formel:
E = p × RRR − (1 − p)        [in R-multiples]
Break-even win rate = 1 / (1 + RRR)
bloecke.erklaerung: The expected value per trade in R. It is only positive if the win rate is above the break-even threshold. The second equation is the first one solved for p with an expected value of zero.
variablen: expected value per trade in R-multiples
win rate, share of winning trades
reward-to-risk ratio: average gain divided by 1R
bloecke.beispiel: With p = 0.40 and RRR = 2, E = 0.40 × 2 − 0.60 = 0.20R per trade. With R = €200 and 100 trades a year, that is €4,000 before costs. Arithmetically, 60 of these trades end in a loss.

bloecke.titel: Break-even win rate by reward-to-risk ratio
bloecke.unter: Break-even win rate p = 1/(1+RRR) before costs. With an RRR of 3, 25% winning trades are enough; with an RRR of 0.5, even two thirds winning trades still bring no profit.

serien.name: Required win rate as a percentage

bloecke.titel: Expected value per trade in R
bloecke.unter: E = p × RRR − (1 − p) before costs and taxes. The zero line runs diagonally through the grid, and only a win rate above the break-even threshold makes up for a poor RRR, which at an RRR of 0.5 means more than two thirds winning trades.

bloecke.md:
## Reference bases for costs and risk

Costs are incurred on the nominal volume, whereas risk is measured against the portfolio. These reference bases diverge, which has a particularly strong effect with tight stops. The assumption is total costs of 0.10% per round turn, consisting of the order fee for buying and selling, half the spread on each side and slippage. The position with a nominal volume of €10,000 from the table above therefore costs €10, that is, 0.05R. The €1,650 position costs €1.65, around 0.008R. For the same risk, the cost burden in R is six times as high.

The break-even win rate shifts accordingly to (1 + k) / (1 + RRR), where k denotes the costs per trade in R. With an RRR of 2, it rises from 33.3% to 35.0%. The difference looks small, but it lies in the range in which good and mediocre systems differ.

Capital income is subject to 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge on that under Section 4 SolzG 1995 (Solidarity Surcharge Act), together 26.375%. With church tax, it is 27.82% or 27.995% respectively. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000 per person and €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG). At the same time, it rules out any deduction of income-related expenses (Werbungskosten), so spending on software, data feeds and seminars does not reduce the tax.

If gains and losses are netted in the same year and in the same loss offset pot (Verlustverrechnungstopf), an expected value of 0.20R falls to around 0.147R after tax. If this is not the case, the tax has an asymmetric effect. Gains are then taxed immediately, but losses may only be offset within their own pot (Section 20(6) EStG).

## Asymmetry of loss and recovery

Loss and recovery are not symmetrical. After a loss of 20%, a gain of 25% is needed to get back to the starting value; after a 50% loss, 100%; and after an 80% loss, 400%. The required gain is DD/(1−DD), where DD denotes the drawdown. This function rises steeply from a drawdown of about 30%.

It follows, purely arithmetically and without psychological assumptions, that an avoided loss is worth more than an additional gain of the same size. The avoided loss preserves the base to which all future percentages refer.

bloecke.titel: Gain needed to return to the previous level
bloecke.unter: According to the formula gain = DD/(1−DD), the required gain is only slightly larger than the loss for losses of up to 20%, and at least twice as large from 50% upwards.

bloecke.titel: Ten consecutive losses at different levels of risk per trade

bloecke.md: With a loss rate of 50% per trade, there is a probability of around 81% that a streak of five losses will occur at least once in 100 independent trades. With a loss rate of 60%, the normal case for a trend-following system, it is 97.6%. Changing strategy because of such a streak is therefore a reaction to chance. Even if the strategy remains unchanged, what such a streak costs must have been worked out in advance. This is the reason why the risk per trade has to be small.

The first mistake is moving the stop. This behaviour has been documented and quantified empirically. In 1998, Odean analysed 10,000 securities accounts and found that gains are realised with a probability of 14.8%, losses with only 9.8%. In addition, the winners that were sold outperformed the losers that were held by 3.4 percentage points in the following year. The meta-analysis by Brown and colleagues (2024) puts the underlying loss aversion at a factor of around 1.96. According to this, a loss weighs roughly twice as heavily as a gain of the same size.

The second mistake is increasing the position size in order to recover losses more quickly. Because of the asymmetry of loss and recovery, this increases the probability of never reaching the starting value again. Leverage does not change the expected value in R-multiples and therefore does not change its sign either. Per euro of equity, however, it multiplies gain, loss and costs to the same extent, and with them the expected value. With a negative expected value, the expected loss therefore grows, and the capital is used up correspondingly faster.

schritte.titel: Set R before opening the chart
schritte.text: A fixed percentage of the portfolio value, usually between 0.5% and 2%. It applies equally to all trades and is adjusted at most once a quarter.
k × ATR(14) below the planned entry or alternatively below the last relevant low, in any case according to a rule that is fixed in advance.
(Capital × risk) / stop distance, rounded down. If the position exceeds a self-imposed share of the portfolio, the number of units is reduced and the stop remains unchanged.

schritte.titel: Limit the total risk of open positions
schritte.text: Cap the sum of all open R, for example at 3R to 5R. Correlated positions count as one, because five technology shares are not five independent positions.

Record the result of each trade as an R-multiple and not in euros. Only after 50 to 100 trades can the win rate and RRR be estimated at all. Before that, any statement about the strategy is based on chance.

bloecke.md: What remains open is how large R itself should be. There is a mathematically optimal solution for this. The Kelly criterion f* = (b × p − q)/b gives the share of capital that maximises the long-term growth rate. However, it assumes that p and b are known, and overestimating these values has serious consequences. In practice, a fraction of it is therefore used. The calculator below shows the relationship. How the criterion works and how high the probability of ruin is are covered in the next lesson.

mitnehmen: The risk per trade is set in euros before entry; the number of units then follows from a simple division.
The stop distance is based on the measured volatility of the security and not on a round number or a fixed percentage.
A win rate only means something together with the reward-to-risk ratio; the break-even win rate is 1/(1+RRR) and rises with costs.
Because loss and recovery are asymmetrical, an avoided loss is worth more than an additional gain of the same size.

Over 100 trades, streaks of five losing trades are the normal case at a win rate of 50% or less, and even at a 60% win rate they still occur with a probability of around 46%, so the position size must be chosen so that such streaks barely affect the portfolio.

begriffe.text: Result of a trade, measured in units of the loss amount set in advance. 1R is the planned loss, and a gain of 2R is twice that amount. Stating results in R makes trades of different sizes and in different markets comparable.
Ratio of the average gain to the amount at risk (1R). Together with the win rate, it determines the expected value E = p × RRR − (1 − p).
Smoothed average of the true range, that is, the price range of a period including price gaps. The ATR measures volatility but not direction, and is used to size stop distances and positions.
Share of winning trades at which the expected value is zero. It is 1/(1 + RRR) before costs and (1 + k)/(1 + RRR) with costs of k R per trade.
Decline from the account's previous peak. The gain needed to recover is DD/(1 − DD) and grows disproportionately. After a 50% loss, a 100% gain is needed.
